claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0 and the Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
In Pulumi, resource ordering is derived from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm installs resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind (per helm/helm pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go).
Helm chart authors cannot declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Pulumi Automation API is a programmatic SDK in every supported language for embedding up, preview, and destroy in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only; other languages must shell out to the helm CLI.

Pulumi Policies is open source, with rules in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego; Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management; the Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Helm docs state: "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's hardcoded kind order begins with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with kinds not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-order list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.
A Helm subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else, so a chart can't express installing one subchart before another.
Helm hooks ordered with helm.sh/hook-weight annotations create resources that Helm doesn't manage as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another or setting the dependsOn resource option creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating dependent resources and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi deletes follow the dependency graph in reverse.
helm.v4.Chart supports the config.kubernetes.io/depends-on annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and dependsOn on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision, and helm rollback restores a prior revision.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and you roll forward by reverting program code and running pulumi up.
Two patterns cover most production deployments of using Pulumi and Helm together.
Pulumi resolves chart values at deploy time and orders the chart install after its dependencies.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program via helm.v4.Chart or helm.v3.Release is the most common adoption pattern.
pulumi convert --from kubernetes converts rendered Helm chart YAML (from helm template) into native Pulumi code.
helm.v4.Chart renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
helm.v3.Release uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges objects from a chart and its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
A Pulumi program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private).
The Pulumi chart values input accepts the same shape as a values.yaml file but lets each leaf be a Pulumi output.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before its dependents, rather than a fixed order by kind.
